claim: The outcome of an encounter with Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) depends on the pathogen's ability to adapt to the variable immune pressures exerted by the host.
source: The outcome of an encounter with Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) depends on the pathogen's ability to adapt to the variable immune pressures exerted by the host.
evidence: This is a general statement about TB pathogenesis that draws from established scientific understanding of host-pathogen interactions.

claim: Experimentally tractable animal models do not recapitulate the heterogeneity of tuberculosis disease.
source: Understanding this interplay has proven difficult, largely because experimentally tractable animal models do not recapitulate the heterogeneity of tuberculosis disease.
evidence: This statement reflects established knowledge about limitations of standard animal models in TB research.

claim: CC strains vary dramatically in their susceptibility to Mtb infection.
source: We report that CC strains vary dramatically in their susceptibility to infection and produce qualitatively distinct immune states.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the CC panel infection study shown in Figure 1.

claim: CC strains produce qualitatively distinct immune states.
source: We report that CC strains vary dramatically in their susceptibility to infection and produce qualitatively distinct immune states.
evidence: This is supported by cytokine profiling and immunological phenotyping data across the CC panel.

claim: Many Mtb virulence pathways are only required in specific host microenvironments.
source: Global analysis of Mtb transposon mutant fitness (TnSeq) across the CC panel revealed that many virulence pathways are only required in specific host microenvironments, identifying a large fraction of the pathogen's genome that has been maintained to ensure fitness in a diverse population.
evidence: This is supported by TnSeq data showing differential bacterial gene requirements across different CC strains.

claim: A large fraction of the Mtb genome has been maintained to ensure fitness in a diverse population.
source: Global analysis of Mtb transposon mutant fitness (TnSeq) across the CC panel revealed that many virulence pathways are only required in specific host microenvironments, identifying a large fraction of the pathogen's genome that has been maintained to ensure fitness in a diverse population.
evidence: This is an inference based on the TnSeq data showing that approximately 750 genes are required across the diverse panel versus ~200 in B6 alone.

claim: Both immunological and bacterial traits can be associated with genetic variants distributed across the mouse genome.
source: Both immunological and bacterial traits can be associated with genetic variants distributed across the mouse genome, making the CC a unique population for identifying specific host-pathogen genetic interactions that influence pathogenesis.
evidence: This is supported by QTL mapping data identifying TipQTL and HipQTL across multiple chromosomes.

claim: Host genetic variation influences immunity to tuberculosis.
source: Classic human genetic studies show that host variation influences immunity to tuberculosis (TB) (Abel et al., 2018; Comstock, 1978).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous human genetic studies.

claim: Co-evolution of Mtb with different populations has produced genetically distinct lineages that demonstrate variable virulence traits.
source: Likewise, the co-evolution of Mtb with different populations across the globe has produced genetically distinct lineages that demonstrate variable virulence traits (Gagneux et al., 2006; Hershberg et al., 2008; Wirth et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on Mtb lineage diversity and virulence.

claim: Interactions between host and pathogen variants may represent an additional determinant of TB outcome.
source: The role of genetic variation on each side of this interaction is established, yet the intimate evolutionary history of both genomes suggests that interactions between host and pathogen variants may represent an additional determinant of outcome (McHenry et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on inference from evolutionary history and cited literature.

claim: Evidence for genetic interactions between host and pathogen genomes have been identified in several infections including TB.
source: Evidence for genetic interactions between host and pathogen genomes have been identified in several infections (Ansari et al., 2017; Berthenet et al., 2018), including TB (Caws et al., 2008; Holt et al., 2018; Thuong et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies demonstrating host-pathogen genetic interactions.

claim: Mice lacking factors necessary for the production of Th1 cells or IFNγ are profoundly susceptible to Mtb infection.
source: Mice lacking factors necessary for the production of Th1 cells or the protective cytokine interferon gamma (IFNγ) are profoundly susceptible to Mtb infection (Caruso et al., 1999; Cooper et al., 1993; Cooper et al., 1997; Flynn et al., 1993; Saunders et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to studies using knockout mice.

claim: Defects in Th1 immunity cause the human syndrome Mendelian Susceptibility to Mycobacterial Disease (MSMD).
source: Defects in this same immune axis cause the human syndrome Mendelian Susceptibility to Mycobacterial Disease (MSMD) (Altare et al., 1998; Bogunovic et al., 2012; Bustamante et al., 2014; Filipe-Santos et al., 2006), demonstrating the value of knockout (KO) mice to characterize genetic variants of large effect.
evidence: This is supported by citations to human genetic studies of MSMD.

claim: The immune response to Mtb in genetically diverse populations is more heterogeneous than any single small animal model.
source: Despite the utility of standard mouse models, it has become increasingly clear that the immune response to Mtb in genetically diverse populations is more heterogeneous than any single small animal model (Smith and Sassetti, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation and represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: A significant fraction of humans exposed to Mtb control the infection without producing a durable IFNγ response.
source: For example, while IFNγ-producing T cells are critical for protective immunity in standard inbred lines of mice, a significant fraction of humans exposed to Mtb control the infection without producing a durable IFNγ response (Lu et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a human study.

claim: IL-17 has little effect on disease progression in B6 mice, except in the context of vaccination or infection with particularly virulent Mtb.
source: Similarly, IL-17 producing T cells have been implicated in both protective responses and inflammatory tissue damage in TB, but IL-17 has little effect on disease progression in B6 mice, except in the context of vaccination or infection with particularly virulent Mtb (Gopal et al., 2012; Khader et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies in B6 mice.

claim: Only a small minority of the >4000 genes retained in the Mtb genome promote fitness in the mouse.
source: The immunological homogeneity of standard mouse models may also explain why only a small minority of the >4000 genes that have been retained in the genome of Mtb during its natural history promote fitness in the mouse (Bellerose et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous TnSeq study and represents an inference about the relationship between host diversity and bacterial gene requirements.

claim: The CC and DO mouse populations more accurately represent the genetic and phenotypic heterogeneity observed in outbred populations.
source: The Collaborative Cross (CC) and Diversity Outbred (DO) mouse populations are new mammalian resources that more accurately represent the genetic and phenotypic heterogeneity observed in outbred populations (Churchill et al., 2004; Churchill et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to papers describing these mouse resources.

claim: DO mice are maintained as an outbred population and each animal represents a unique and largely heterozygous genome.
source: DO mice are maintained as an outbred population and each animal represents a unique and largely heterozygous genome (Keller et al., 2018; Svenson et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations describing the DO population structure.

claim: Each inbred CC strain's genome is almost entirely homozygous, producing a genetically stable and reproducible population.
source: In contrast, each inbred CC strain's genome is almost entirely homozygous, producing a genetically stable and reproducible population in which the phenotypic effect of recessive mutations is maximized (Shorter et al., 2019; Srivastava et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations describing the CC population structure.

claim: DO mice have been used to identify correlates of TB disease that resemble those observed in non-human primates and humans.
source: In the context of TB, DO mice have been used as individual, unique hosts to identify correlates of disease, which resemble those observed in non-human primates and humans (Ahmed et al., 2020; Gopal et al., 2013; Koyuncu et al., 2021; Niazi et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous DO studies in TB.

claim: Small panels of CC strains have been used to identify host background as a determinant of BCG vaccination efficacy.
source: Small panels of the reproducible CC strains have been leveraged to identify host background as a determinant of the protective efficacy of BCG vaccination (Smith et al., 2016) and a specific variant underlying protective immunity to tuberculosis (Smith et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous CC studies.

claim: A panel of 52 CC lines and eight founder strains were infected with Mtb via the intravenous route with a saturated library of transposon mutants.
source: To characterize the diversity of disease states that are possible in a genetically diverse mouse population, we infected a panel of 52 CC lines and the eight founder strains with Mtb. To enable bacterial transposon sequencing (TnSeq) studies downstream, the animals were infected via the intravenous (IV) route with a saturated library of Mtb transposon mutants (infectious dose of 105 CFU), which in sum produce an infection that is similar to the wild-type parental strain (Bellerose et al., 2020; Sassetti and Rubin, 2003).
evidence: This describes the experimental design and is supported by the data presented.

claim: Groups of three to six male mice per genotype were infected and TB disease-related traits were quantified at one-month post-infection.
source: Groups of three to six male mice per genotype were infected and TB disease-related traits were quantified at one-month post-infection.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: Bacterial burden measured by CFU and CEQ were highly correlated (r = 0.88).
source: The bacterial burden after 4 weeks of infection was assessed by plating (colony-forming units, CFU) and quantifying the number of bacterial chromosomes in the tissue (chromosome equivalents, CEQ). These two metrics were highly correlated (r = 0.88) and revealed a wide variation in bacterial burden across the panel (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing CFU and CEQ measurements.

claim: Lung bacterial burden varied by more than 1000-fold across the CC panel.
source: Across the entire CC panel, lung bacterial burden varied by more than 1000-fold, ranging from animals that are significantly more resistant than B6, to mice that harbored more than 109 bacteria in their lungs (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by CFU data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Bacterial burden in the spleen varied several thousand-fold across the panel and was moderately correlated with lung burden (r = 0.43).
source: Bacterial burden in the spleen also varied several thousand-fold across the panel and was moderately correlated with lung burden (r = 0.43) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by spleen CFU data and correlation analysis.

claim: Lung CFU was strongly correlated with weight loss and proinflammatory cytokines including CXCL2, CCL3, G-CSF, CXCL1, IL-6, and IL-1α.
source: Lung CFU was strongly correlated with weight loss, mediators that enhance neutrophil differentiation or migration (CXCL2 (MIP-2; r = 0.79), CCL3 (MIP-1a; r = 0.77), G-CSF (r = 0.78), and CXCL1 (KC; r = 0.76)), and more general proinflammatory cytokines (IL-6 (r = 0.80) and IL-1α (r = 0.76)) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis of CFU and cytokine data.

claim: The heritability of immunological and disease traits ranged from 56%–87% with a mean of 73.4%.
source: The reproducibility of CC genotypes allowed us to quantitatively assess the heritability (h2) of these immunological and disease traits. The percent of the variation attributed to genotype ranged from 56%–87% (mean = 73.4%; (Appendix 1—table 1)).
evidence: This is supported by heritability calculations from the CC panel data.

claim: CC030/GeniUnc, CC040/TauUnc and A/J lost more weight than their bacterial burdens would predict.
source: In particular, CC030/GeniUnc (p = 0.003), CC040/TauUnc (p = 0.027) and A/J (p = 0.03) lost more weight than their bacterial burdens would predict (Figure 1C; noted by #).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of weight loss versus CFU shown in Figure 1C.

claim: IFNγ and interferon-inducible chemokines were notably unrelated to bacterial burden (R < 0.3).
source: The cluster of cytokines that was most notably unrelated to bacterial burden included IFNγ and the interferon-inducible chemokines CXCL10 (IP10), CXCL9 (MIG), and CCL5 (RANTES) (Red cluster in Figure 1B; Figure 1—figure supplement 1) (R < 0.3).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: A number of genotypes were able to control bacterial replication yet had very low levels of IFNγ.
source: While high IFNγ levels in susceptible animals was therefore expected, it was more surprising to find a number of genotypes that were able to control bacterial replication yet had very low levels of this critically important cytokine (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1D plotting IFNγ versus lung CFU.

claim: Four CC genotypes (CC027, CC032, CC037, and CC042) were susceptible by aerosol infection, validating findings from IV infection.
source: To assess the reproducibility of these findings in an aerosol infection model, we tested four CC genotypes that were susceptible by IV infection, including CC027, CC032, CC037, and CC042. We infected groups of 4–6 mice per genotype with H37Rv strain via low-dose aerosol infection (~100 CFU), including B6 mice as resistant controls. At 4-weeks post infection, we quantified lung CFU, lung cytokine abundance and weight loss as measurements of TB disease. Compared to the resistant B6 mice, the selected CC strains demonstrated higher bacterial burden in the lung (Figure 1E) and significant weight loss (Figure 1F), thus validating disease traits as consistent across both route and dose.
evidence: This is supported by aerosol infection data shown in Figure 1E-H.

claim: CXCL1 was highly correlated with lung burden by both IV (R = 0.76) and aerosol (R = 0.92) routes.
source: Notably, CXCL1 was consistently high in the susceptible genotypes, as compared to B6 (Figure 1G), and was highly correlated with lung burden by both IV (R = 0.76) and aerosol (R = 0.92) routes.
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis of CXCL1 and CFU data from both infection routes.

claim: Nine individual TB disease or cytokine traits were associated with chromosomal loci (TipQTL).
source: Of the 32 TB-disease traits, we identified nine individual metrics that were associated with a chromosomal locus. Of these, three were associated with high confidence (p ≤ 0.053), and six other QTL met a suggestive threshold as determined by permutation analysis (p < 0.2; Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by QTL mapping analysis shown in Table 1 and Figure 2.

claim: Spleen CFU and spleen CEQ were associated with the same interval on distal chromosome 2 (Tip5).
source: For example, spleen CFU and spleen CEQ, which are both measures of bacterial burden and highly correlated, were associated with the same interval on distal chromosome 2 (Table 1, Tip5; Figure 2A and C).
evidence: This is supported by QTL mapping data shown in Figure 2A and C and Table 1.

claim: IL-10 abundance was associated with two distinct QTL, one of which fell within the Tip5 bacterial burden interval on chromosome 2.
source: IL-10 abundance was associated with two distinct QTL (Table 1). While IL-10 was only moderately correlated with spleen CFU (R = 0.48), one of its QTL fell within the Tip5 bacterial burden interval on chromosome 2 (Figure 2A and C).
evidence: This is supported by QTL mapping data shown in Figure 2A and C and Table 1.

claim: At Tip5, the NOD haplotype was associated with high values for spleen CFU, spleen CEQ, and IL-10.
source: At this QTL, the NOD haplotype was associated with high values for all three traits (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by haplotype effect analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claim: CXCL1 abundance and lung CFU were individually associated to the same region on chromosome 7 (Tip8).
source: Similarly, the strongly correlated traits, CXCL1 abundance and lung CFU, were individually associated to the same region on chromosome 7 (Table 1, Tip8; Figure 2B and D).
evidence: This is supported by QTL mapping data shown in Figure 2B and D and Table 1.

claim: At Tip8, the CAST haplotype was associated with both low bacterial burden and CXCL1.
source: In this interval, the CAST haplotype was associated with both low bacterial burden and CXCL1 (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by haplotype effect analysis shown in Figure 2F.

claim: An F2 intercross validation study identified a QTL on chromosome 7 that overlapped with Tip8.
source: We identified a QTL significantly associated with lung CFU (LOD = 6.81; p < 0.05; 10,000 permutations) on chromosome seven that overlapped with Tip8 (peak position Chr7:28.6 Mb), thus validating this locus as a main driver of bacterial burden.
evidence: This is supported by QTL mapping in the F2 population shown in Figure 3C.

claim: 214 Mtb genes are required for growth or survival in B6 mice.
source: From this TnSeq screen, we identified 214 Mtb genes that are required for growth or survival of Mtb in B6 mice, based on significant underrepresentation of the corresponding mutant after four weeks of in vivo selection.
evidence: This is supported by TnSeq analysis in B6 mice.

claim: 87% of genes required in B6 overlapped with a similar previous analysis in BALB/c mice.
source: Eighty-seven percent of these genes overlapped with a similar previous analysis in BALB/c mice (Bellerose et al., 2020) highlighting the specificity of the analysis.
evidence: This is supported by comparison with a cited previous study.

claim: The cumulative number of bacterial genes necessary for growth plateaued at ~750 after inclusion of approximately 20–25 mouse genotypes.
source: As more CC strains, and presumably more distinct immune states, were included in the analysis, the cumulative number of bacterial genes necessary for growth in these animals also increased. This cumulative gene set plateaued at ~750, after the inclusion of approximately 20–25 mouse genotypes (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by cumulative gene count analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The number of genes important for fitness in the CC panel far outnumbered the 380 genes identified in B6 and immunodeficient KO strains combined.
source: The number of genes important for fitness in the CC panel far outnumbered the 380 genes identified in the B6 and immunodeficient KO strains combined (Figure 4B and Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by Venn diagram analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: TnSeq predictions were validated using deletion mutants in a mini-pool infection experiment.
source: To verify that our TnSeq study accurately assessed the effect of the corresponding loss-of-function alleles, we assessed the phenotypes of selected bacterial deletion mutants in a small set of mouse genotypes that were predicted to produce differential selection. Individual Mtb mutants lacking genes necessary for ESX-1 Type VII secretion (eccB1), siderophore-mediated iron acquisition (mbtA), phosphate transport (pstC2), glycerol catabolism (glpK), and RNA processing (rnaseJ) were generated and tagged with a unique molecular barcode.
evidence: This is supported by mini-pool validation data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: In each case, the difference in relative abundance predicted by TnSeq was reproduced with deletion mutants.
source: In each case, the difference in relative abundance predicted by TnSeq was reproduced with deletion mutants.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of TnSeq and mini-pool data in Figure 4C.

claim: The ΔbioA mutant was less attenuated in CAST background than in B6 strain as predicted by TnSeq.
source: bioA is necessary for biotin production and is essential for growth in B6 mice (Woong Park et al., 2011). Our TnSeq study (Figure 4—source data 1) predicted this mutant was less attenuated in the CAST background (ratio of input/selected = 12.1) than in the B6 strain (ratio of input/selected = 42.2). Two weeks after aerosol infection, we found that the ∆bioA mutant was cleared from the lungs and spleen of B6 mice but displayed similar growth to wild-type in the lungs of CAST mice (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by aerosol infection data with ΔbioA mutant shown in Figure 4D.

claim: There are 136 'core' virulence functions required in the majority of mouse genotypes and 607 'adaptive' virulence genes required in only a subset of lines.
source: The distribution of Mtb's requirements across the mouse panel suggested the presence of two broad categories of genes. A set of 136 'core' virulence functions were required in the majority of mouse genotypes, and a second larger set of 607 'adaptive' virulence genes were required in only a subset of lines (Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is based on analysis of TnSeq data across the CC panel.

claim: ESX1 mutants were attenuated for growth in B6 mice, and this requirement was enhanced in mice lacking Rag2, Ifng, or Nos2.
source: Mutants lacking the major structural components of the ESX1 system were attenuated for growth in B6 mice, as expected. This requirement was enhanced in mice lacking Rag2, Ifng, or Nos2 (Figure 4E), consistent with the preferential role of ESX1 during the initial stage of infection before the initiation of adaptive immunity (Stanley et al., 2003), which is prolonged in these immunodeficient strains.
evidence: This is supported by TnSeq data shown in Figure 4E and cited literature.

claim: The attenuation of glnQ mutants was relieved in all four immunodeficient mouse lines.
source: In contrast, the attenuation of mutants lacking the glnQ encoded glutamine uptake system was relieved in all four immunodeficient mouse lines (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by TnSeq data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: ahpC and ahpD mutations had no effect in any of the B6-derived strains, but ahpC mutants were highly attenuated in a small number of CC strains.
source: However, deletion of ahpC has no effect on Mtb replication in B6 or BALB/c mice (Springer et al., 2001), and we confirmed that ahpC and ahpD mutations had no effect in any of the B6-derived strains. In contrast, ahpC, but not ahpD mutants were highly attenuated in a small number of CC strains (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by TnSeq data shown in Figure 4E and cited literature.

claim: plcD mutants were specifically underrepresented in a number of CC mice but not in B6-derived KO mouse strains.
source: Similarly, the four phospholipase C enzymes of Mtb (plcA-D) are implicated in both fatty acid uptake and modifying host cell membranes but are dispensable for replication in B6 mice (Le Chevalier et al., 2015). Again, while we found that none of these genes were required in B6-derived KO mouse strains, the plcD mutants were specifically underrepresented in a number of CC mice (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by TnSeq data shown in Figure 4E and cited literature.

claim: sigC, sigI, sigF, sigL, and sigM mutants were each significantly underrepresented in multiple strains of mice.
source: Our study assessed the importance of each sigma factor in parallel across diverse host genotypes and identified a clear role for several of these regulators. sigC, sigI, sigF, sigL, and sigM mutants were each significantly underrepresented in multiple strains of mice, and several of these phenotypes were only apparent in the diverse CC animals (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by TnSeq data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Approximately three times more genes contribute to bacterial growth or survival in the CC population than in the standard B6 model.
source: Overall, we find that approximately three times more genes contribute to bacterial growth or survival in the CC population than in the standard B6 model.
evidence: This is based on comparison of gene counts from TnSeq analysis in B6 versus the CC panel.

claim: 679 mutants varied significantly (FDR < 5%) in at least two independent pairwise comparisons across the host panel.
source: Upon performing each possible pairwise comparison between the in vivo selected mutant pools, we found 679 mutants whose representation varied significantly (FDR < 5%) in at least two independent comparisons (Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of TnSeq data.

claim: Weighted gene correlation network analysis divided the 679 variable mutants into 20 internally-correlated modules.
source: We then applied weighted gene correlation network analysis (WGCNA) (Langfelder and Horvath, 2008) to divide the mutants into 20 internally-correlated modules.
evidence: This is supported by WGCNA analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Nearly all modules contained genes that are encoded adjacently in the genome and many consisted of genes dedicated to a single virulence-associated function.
source: Further enrichment of these modules for the most representative genes (intramodular connectivity >0.6) revealed that nearly all modules contained genes that are encoded adjacently in the genome and many of these modules consisted of genes dedicated to a single virulence-associated function (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by module composition analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Module 3 contains genes necessary for ESX1-mediated protein secretion.
source: Module three contains two distally encoded loci both known to be necessary for ESX1-mediated protein secretion, the primary ESX1 locus (rv3868-rv3883) and the espACD operon (rv3616c-rv3614c).
evidence: This is supported by module composition shown in Figure 5A and established knowledge of ESX1 function.

claim: Module 6 was highly enriched for mutants predicted to be involved in oxidative stress resistance.
source: The 20 genes assigned to Module six included two components of an important oxidative stress resistance complex (sseA and rv3005c) and were highly enriched for mutants predicted to be involved in this same process via genetic interaction mapping (11/20 genes were identified in Nambi et al., 2015, a statistically significant overlap [p < 2.8e-10 by hypergeometric test]).
evidence: This is supported by module composition analysis and statistical comparison with a cited study.

claim: Mouse genotypes were clustered into six major groups based on TnSeq profiles of 679 differentially fit Mtb mutants.
source: To explore the complexity of immune environments in the CC, we used the TnSeq profiles of the 679 differentially fit Mtb mutants to cluster the mouse panel into six major groups of host genotypes (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by clustering analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: One mouse cluster (Cluster F) was significantly associated with high CFU and contained susceptible immunodeficient animals.
source: One mouse cluster was significantly associated with high CFU (Cluster F, Figure 5B), which contained susceptible Nos2-/-, Cybb-/-, Ifng -/-, and Rag2-/- animals.
evidence: This is supported by cluster analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The high CFU cluster was associated with increased requirement for lipid uptake (Modules 5 and 16) and ESX1.
source: This high CFU cluster was associated with alterations in a diverse set of bacterial modules and corresponded to an increased requirement for lipid uptake (Modules 5 and 16) and ESX1, consistent with previous TnSeq studies in susceptible Nos2-/- and C3HeB/FeJ mice (Mishra et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by module association analysis and cited literature.

claim: A significant reduction in the requirement for oxidative stress resistance (Module 6) was identified in the highest CFU cluster.
source: In addition, we identified a significant reduction in the requirement for the oxidative stress resistance (Module 6) in the highest CFU cluster.
evidence: This is supported by module association analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: 41 HipQTL reached an unadjusted p-value threshold of 0.05 for single Mtb mutant traits.
source: When the relative abundance of each Mtb mutant phenotype was considered individually, the corresponding 'Host Interacting with Pathogen QTL' (HipQTL) were distributed across the mouse genome (Figure 6A). Forty-one of these traits reached an unadjusted p-value threshold of 0.05 and can be considered as robust for single hypothesis testing (Hip1-41, Table 2).
evidence: This is supported by QTL mapping of individual mutant traits shown in Figure 6A and Table 2.

claim: Three module eigentraits (Module 3, 4, and 16) were associated with QTL at a similar position on chromosome 10.
source: Three of these 'eigentraits' were associated with QTL at a similar position on chromosome 10 (Figure 6B), corresponding to Module 3 (TypeVII secretion, ESX1), Module 4 (mycobactin synthesis, mbt), or Module 16 (cholesterol uptake, mce4).
evidence: This is supported by QTL mapping of module eigentraits shown in Figure 6B.

claim: A single genetic variant controlled the abundance of ESX1 and mbt mutants (Hip42).
source: Both the relative positions of the module-associated QTL and the associated founder haplotypes indicated that a single genetic variant controlled the abundance of ESX1 and mbt mutants (Hip42). Specifically, we found no statistical support for differentiating these QTL based on position (p = 0.93) (Boehm et al., 2019) and the same founder haplotypes were associated with extreme trait values at both loci, though they had opposite effects on the abundance of ESX1 mutants and mbt mutants (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of QTL positions and haplotype effects shown in Figure 6F.

claim: A single haplotype has a pleiotropic effect on Mtb's environment and has opposing effects on the requirement for mycobactin synthesis and ESX1 secretion.
source: We conclude that a single haplotype has a pleiotropic effect on Mtb's environment and has opposing effects of the requirement for mycobactin synthesis and ESX1 secretion.
evidence: This is an inference based on the QTL mapping and haplotype effect data.

claim: Two TipQTL overlapped with HipQTL (Tip5/Hip4 on chromosome 2 and Tip9/Hip35 on chromosome 17).
source: Two TipQTL overlapped with HipQTL (Figure 7; Tip5/Hip4 on chromosome two and Tip9/Hip35 on chromosome 17), suggesting specific interactions between bacterial fitness and immunity.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of TipQTL and HipQTL positions shown in Figure 7.

claim: Founder haplotypes at Hip42 could differentiate CC strains with significantly altered total bacterial burden.
source: We found that the founder haplotypes associated with extreme trait values at this QTL could differentiate CC strains with significantly altered total bacterial burden, and the NOD and WSB haplotypes were associated with higher bacterial numbers (p = 0.0085 for spleen CEQ; P = 0.027 for spleen CFU; Figure 6H).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of bacterial burden stratified by haplotype shown in Figure 6H.

claim: For Tip5 QTL, cathepsin Z (Ctsz) is a candidate gene that encodes a lysosomal cysteine proteinase and has been associated with TB disease risk in humans.
source: For the Tip5 QTL underlying CEQ, CFU, and IL-10 levels, we identified nine candidate genes with regulatory or splicing variants and two genes with missense variants specific to the NOD haplotype. Of these candidates, cathepsin Z (Ctsz) encodes a lysosomal cysteine proteinase and has previously been associated with TB disease risk in humans (Adams et al., 2011; Cooke et al., 2008).
evidence: This is based on candidate gene prioritization and cited human genetic studies.

claim: The QTL underlying lung CFU and CXCL1 abundance (Tip8) contained over 50 candidate genes.
source: The QTL underlying lung CFU and CXCL1 abundance (Tip8), which was driven solely by the genetically divergent CAST founder haplotype, contained over 50 genes (Table 3) and will need further refinement.
evidence: This is based on candidate gene prioritization shown in Table 3.

claim: Within Hip42 interval, Rhobtb1 is supported as a candidate gene with a missense mutation and variants in the 3' UTR following the AJ/B6 haplotype pattern.
source: For the AJ/B6 haplotype state, we identified a missense mutation and several variants in the 3' UTR of Rhobtb1, which belongs to the Rho family of the Ras superfamily of small GTPases (Goitre et al., 2014). Overall, the evidence supports a role for Rhobtb1 in a monogenic effect at the chromosome 10 locus.
evidence: This is based on candidate gene prioritization and cited literature on Rhobtb1 function.

claim: The CC panel encompasses a broad spectrum of TB susceptibility and immune phenotypes.
source: Using over 60 diverse mouse strains, we report that the CC panel encompasses a broad spectrum of TB susceptibility and immune phenotypes.
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by the overall findings from the CC panel characterization.

claim: Approximately three times more bacterial genes contribute to fitness in the diverse panel than in any single mouse strain.
source: We report that approximately three times more bacterial genes contribute to fitness in the diverse panel than in any single mouse strain, defining a large fraction of the bacterial genome that is dedicated to adapting to distinct immune states.
evidence: This is supported by TnSeq analysis comparing gene requirements across the CC panel versus individual strains.

claim: A large fraction of the pathogen's genome is dedicated to adapting to distinct immune states.
source: We report that approximately three times more bacterial genes contribute to fitness in the diverse panel than in any single mouse strain, defining a large fraction of the bacterial genome that is dedicated to adapting to distinct immune states.
evidence: This is an inference based on the TnSeq findings showing differential gene requirements across diverse hosts.

claim: The CC population is a tractable model for identifying specific host-pathogen genetic interactions that influence pathogenesis.
source: Together, these observations support the CC population as a tractable model of host diversity that greatly expands the spectrum of immunological and pathological states that can be modeled in the mouse.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the overall findings of the study.
